questions.q: In orders.csv, what is the total line_total (quantity x unit_price) for the Footwear category, including all orders regardless of status?
questions.explain: Orders 1001, 1004, 1008, 1013, and 1017 sum to $909.93 — before excluding the cancelled and returned orders.

questions.q: Why does Footwear's revenue drop to $649.95 once you filter for status == "Shipped" before grouping?
options: Filtering by status removes all Footwear orders from the dataset
It excludes order 1004 (Cancelled) and order 1008 (Returned), both Footwear orders that shouldn't count as real sold revenue
$649.95 is actually incorrect — $909.93 is the right number regardless of status
groupby() automatically excludes cancelled orders with no filtering needed
questions.explain: groupby() summarizes whatever rows it's given — deciding which rows belong in the summary is a separate, necessary step.

questions.q: What does named aggregation syntax like df.groupby("category").agg(total_revenue=("line_total", "sum")) provide?
options: Several summary statistics computed in one call, each with a clear, custom output column name
A way to filter rows before grouping
A guarantee that no column will contain missing values
Automatic conversion of all columns to numeric types
questions.explain: Named aggregation lets you compute multiple stats (count, sum, mean, etc.) in a single, readable .agg() call.

questions.q: According to df.groupby("status")["order_id"].count() on orders.csv, how many orders have status "Shipped"?
questions.explain: Of the 20 orders, 1 is Cancelled (1004) and 1 is Returned (1008), leaving 18 as Shipped.

questions.q: After filtering orders.csv for status == "Shipped" and quantity >= 0, what is the total line_total across all categories?
questions.explain: Excluding the Cancelled order (1004), the Returned order (1008), and the negative-quantity row (1014) brings the raw $2,750.43 total down to $2,512.45.
